analysis.one_liner: Bans employers and job agencies from refusing to hire someone because they are unemployed.
analysis.headline: The bill got no action beyond its referral to committee in January 2014 and died when the 113th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for employers with 15 or more employees, staffing agencies, and job-posting websites to refuse to consider or hire someone — or to advertise jobs saying the unemployed need not apply — because of their current or past unemployment. It gives the Labor Department power to investigate complaints and gives workers the right to sue for lost wages, extra damages, and their job back. The bill applies to federal agencies too. It never left the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed job seekers — especially the long-term unemployed, who during the slow recovery after the Great Recession faced job ads explicitly excluding them — would gain a legal right to be considered on their merits and to sue for lost wages and other damages. The bill's findings state that excluding the unemployed wastes skills, raises unemployment insurance payouts, and lowers tax revenues.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for employers with 15 or more employees to refuse to consider or hire someone because they are unemployed, and bans job ads stating that unemployment disqualifies an applicant.
Applies the same ban to employment agencies, recruiters, and websites that publish job ads, including rules against screening, sorting, or limiting job information by unemployment status.

Lets affected workers — or someone acting for them and others similarly situated — sue in federal or state court for lost wages, liquidated damages, punitive damages, and equitable relief including being hired, with attorney's fees paid by the losing employer.

Directs the Labor Secretary to receive, investigate, and try to resolve complaints under Fair Labor Standards Act procedures, and to pay recovered sums directly to affected workers; applies the same ban to federal employing agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees and staffing firms or job boards would bear new compliance obligations and legal exposure: actual damages doubled as liquidated damages, punitive damages, at least $250 per violation in civil penalties for retaliating against workers, and the plaintiff's attorney fees. The cost is real but capped in scope — firms under 15 employees are exempt, and employers can reduce liability by proving good faith.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mid-size and large employers and staffing firms

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles actual damages as automatic liquidated damages and allows punitive damages and suits on behalf of groups of similarly situated workers, which would expose even careful employers to expensive litigation over routine hiring decisions.
Where no wages were lost, the bill sets a floor of $1,000 per violation per day, a penalty that could grow quickly in disputes over hiring decisions that are hard to reconstruct.
Enforcement depends heavily on individual lawsuits and Labor Department action, so outcomes would vary with how aggressively the agency of the day pursues complaints.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real, documented practice of the era — ads stating that the unemployed would not be considered — and the bill includes guardrails: a bona fide occupational qualification exception when recent related experience genuinely matters for the job, an exemption for employers under 15 employees, and reduced damages for good-faith employers. The main cost is litigation exposure for mid-size and large employers and staffing firms. The trade-off is defensible on its face, though the $1,000-per-day floor and doubled damages are designed to be punishing rather than merely compensatory.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 29, 2014, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Fair Employment Opportunity Act of 2014 in the Senate on January 29, 2014, joined by Senators Markey, Gillibrand, Shaheen, Sanders, and Murphy.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral is the last action recorded in the bill's history.
Eight senators cosponsored the bill — 7 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican signed on.
The committee never held a markup, reported the bill, or brought it to a vote, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 without the bill ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more employees, staffing agencies, and job-posting sites avoided new litigation exposure and compliance rules, while long-term unemployed workers gained no new legal protection. Members of Congress who never acted faced no vote on the question either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and staffing firms; no new hiring rules

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill creates a private right of action with doubled damages, punitive damages, and fee-shifting for hiring decisions based on unemployment. Their interest in unrestricted hiring discretion runs against the interest of unemployed job seekers in being considered.

The bill regulates these firms directly — banning screening, sorting, or referral by unemployment status and banning ads that disqualify the unemployed. Their screening practices are the mechanism the bill targets.
The bill's findings argue that excluding the unemployed from hiring increases demand for unemployment benefits and strains trust funds, so re-employment would reduce those outlays.
